messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 51
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: School Principal
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 56

**Patient Vignette: Mr. A.**

Mr. A. is a 51-year-old North American man, a widower, who has been the principal of a mid-sized public elementary school for the past twelve years. He presents as a composed, articulate man, dressed in a pressed button-down and slacks, though there is a noticeable tremor in his hands when he reaches for the water glass on the table. He begins by apologizing for his "short fuse" at work lately, a trait he says is "completely unlike" the man he used to be.

The story begins eighteen months ago. Mr. A. had always been the picture of health—a former collegiate athlete who still ran five miles every morning before the school day began. During a routine physical, his doctor noted an irregularity. What followed was a blur of appointments, scans, and a word that now feels like a physical blow: **cancer**. Stage III colorectal cancer. He remembers the precise moment the oncologist said the word, the way the overhead fluorescent light flickered, and the smell of antiseptic hand sanitizer in the room. He felt, he says, as though he had been "unplugged from the world." The floor felt like it was tilting.

The treatment was brutal. Surgery, followed by six months of aggressive chemotherapy. He tried to maintain his role as principal, working from a hospital bed in his office during the worst of the infusions, the chemo pump a constant, humming reminder in his pocket. He felt a desperate need to project normalcy, to be the steady anchor for his staff and 800 students. But inside, he was drowning. He remembers the night he vomited so violently he thought his stitches would burst, and the terror that he would die alone in his bathroom, his wife having passed away from a heart attack five years prior.

Now, the cancer is in remission. The scans are clean. His doctors have given him a clean bill of health. But Mr. A. does not feel healed. He feels hollowed out.

His days are now governed by a relentless, exhausting vigilance. He cannot sit through a faculty meeting without his mind drifting to the sensation of a new lump, a phantom ache, a sudden fatigue. Every minor physical sensation—a headache, a muscle twinge, a stomach gurgle—is a potential herald of the disease's return. He has become a hyper-vigilant scanner of his own body, a job he performs dozens of times a day. He has visited his primary care physician eight times in the last three months for non-specific complaints, each time leaving with a "you're fine" that offers no comfort, only a temporary reprieve before the next worry cycle begins.

The most profound change is his relationship with time. He used to be a planner, a man who looked forward to retirement and grandkids. Now, he cannot look ahead. He cancelled his subscription to a travel magazine because the images of future vacations felt like a cruel joke. He finds it impossible to imagine himself alive in a year. When a teacher asks about a curriculum plan for the fall semester, a cold dread settles in his stomach; he feels a profound, irrational certainty that he will not be there to see it through.

He has also become irritable, a trait that terrifies him. Last week, a first-grader accidentally knocked over a stack of papers on his desk. Mr. A. felt a surge of white-hot rage that was entirely disproportionate. He didn't yell, but he saw the child's face crumple in fear. He apologized profusely, but the image of the child's frightened face haunts him. He sees in that child's eyes a reflection of his own vulnerability, a fragility he cannot bear.

Sleep is a battleground. He avoids it, because sleep brings the dreams. Not nightmares of monsters, but vivid, clinical replays: the cold gel of the ultrasound, the claustrophobic hum of the MRI machine, the metallic taste of the chemo. He wakes in a cold sweat, his heart hammering, disoriented, reaching for a wife who is no longer there. He spends the small hours of the night walking the darkened halls of his own home, checking his pulse, checking the locks, checking for a threat he cannot name but feels with absolute certainty is coming for him. He is a man who survived, but who has not yet returned to the land of the living.
